cim: OCC Issues Supervisory Framework for Banks’ Use of “Super Intelligence”: A Risk-Based Approach to Generative and Agentic AI
kihagyva: P3: 62 pont, tendencia 20%, jóváhagyás után fordul
cim_eredeti: OCC Issues Supervisory Framework for Banks’ Use of “Super Intelligence”: A Risk-Based Approach to Generative and Agentic AI
szoveg_eredeti:
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has taken another important step in addressing the rapidly expanding use of artificial intelligence in the banking industry. On November 4, 2026, the OCC issued a new supervisory framework designed to assist its bank examiners in evaluating banks’ use of what the agency, following the terminology adopted by the Trump Administration, calls “Super Intelligence” (SI). The framework focuses particularly on generative AI and agentic AI and provides examiners with a detailed roadmap for evaluating the risks associated with these technologies and the controls banks have implemented to manage those risks.

Importantly, the OCC emphasizes that the framework is intended as a resource for examiners, not as a source of new regulatory requirements for banks. It does not establish a separate category of supervisory risk for SI, require banks to adopt a separate SI risk appetite, or impose new enforceable standards. Rather, it directs examiners to consider how the use of SI may introduce, amplify, or modify risks that banks already manage under established supervisory frameworks.

That distinction is significant, particularly at a time when financial institutions are seeking greater regulatory clarity concerning the use of generative and agentic AI.

The OCC’s approach: Technology-neutral supervision rather than a new regulatory regime

The new framework implements the OCC’s commitment to encourage responsible technological innovation while maintaining the safety and soundness of the banking system and compliance with applicable laws and regulations.

The OCC recognizes that SI can provide substantial benefits to banks and their customers, including more efficient customer service, improved fraud detection, stronger cybersecurity, reduced operational costs, and greater automation of manual processes. At the same time, the agency acknowledges that the rapid evolution of generative and agentic AI presents risks that may not be adequately addressed by controls developed for traditional technologies.

The OCC makes clear, however, that examiners should not treat SI as a separate and distinct risk category. Nor should banks be required to establish a separate SI risk appetite. Instead, SI-related risks should be incorporated into existing risk-management frameworks, including those addressing operational risk, compliance risk, credit risk, model risk, cybersecurity, privacy, and third-party relationships.

This approach is consistent with the OCC’s broader emphasis on technology-neutral supervision. The agency intends to evaluate the risks presented by a particular application rather than impose restrictions merely because a bank employs a new or sophisticated technology.

The OCC also emphasizes proportionality. Examiners should exercise judgment based on the bank’s size, complexity, risk profile, and the nature and potential consequences of its particular SI applications.

The framework identifies six principal pillars around which examiners should organize their evaluation of a bank’s use of SI:

The OCC translates these six pillars into sixteen supervisory components, addressing such matters as governance and accountability, model risk management, data governance, privacy, compliance, vendor risk, operational resilience, cybersecurity, performance monitoring, testing, documentation, internal audit, and reporting.

Although many of these subjects are familiar to bank compliance and risk-management professionals, the framework identifies important considerations arising from the distinctive characteristics of generative and agentic AI.

For example, the OCC recognizes that conventional model validation may be insufficient for systems that produce non-deterministic outputs, undergo frequent changes, or rely on third-party foundation models. It therefore encourages testing that takes account of changing model behavior, hallucinations, adversarial inputs, and the possibility that a system may behave differently when exposed to similar prompts.

The framework also recognizes that an AI system may continue operating normally from a technical standpoint while taking inappropriate or harmful actions. Banks therefore should consider safeguards such as circuit breakers, rate limits, restricted permissions, fallback procedures, and mechanisms for suspending or terminating an agent’s activities.

The significance of agentic AI and human oversight

One of the most important aspects of the framework is its recognition that the risks associated with AI depend not simply on the sophistication of the underlying technology but also on the degree of autonomy the system possesses and the consequences of its actions.

The OCC explains that a relatively simple rules-based agent authorized to initiate transactions may present greater risk than a sophisticated model used solely for internal drafting assistance.

The framework distinguishes between human-in-the-loop controls, under which a human reviews and approves an output or action before it is implemented, and human-on-the-loop controls, under which a human actively monitors an independently operating system and has the practical ability to intervene.

The degree of human involvement should be calibrated to the potential consequences of the system’s actions, the extent of its autonomy, and the reversibility of those actions.

Importantly, the OCC cautions against treating human oversight as a merely formal exercise. A designated reviewer must have the necessary expertise, information, authority, and capacity to evaluate, reject, modify, or halt the system’s actions. A nominal approval process that amounts to little more than clicking a button will not necessarily provide meaningful oversight.

These considerations are particularly important as banks move beyond using generative AI as an internal productivity tool and begin deploying agents capable of interacting with customers, accessing accounts, initiating transactions, and performing other functions with limited human intervention.

Consumer compliance receives particular attention

Of particular interest to the consumer financial services industry is the framework’s treatment of consumer compliance risk.

The OCC expressly recognizes that SI used in customer service, marketing, servicing, collections, disclosures, and other consumer-facing activities can create compliance risks when outputs are materially inaccurate, misleading, or inconsistent with the terms of the bank’s products.

The framework specifically identifies hallucinations concerning fees, interest rates, account status, and bank policies as potential sources of legal liability and customer harm. Banks are encouraged to implement controls that limit automated representations, require verification in higher-impact situations, and facilitate prompt correction and remediation when inaccurate information is provided.

This is an important recognition of the practical challenges associated with deploying generative AI in consumer financial services. A customer-service agent that confidently provides incorrect information about an account balance, payment obligation, interest rate, or fee can create consequences that extend beyond customer dissatisfaction. Depending on the circumstances, the conduct could implicate existing federal and state consumer financial protection laws.

The OCC also recognizes that the use of SI does not change a bank’s underlying legal obligations. Rather, banks must ensure that their use of the technology is consistent with applicable laws and regulations.

That observation should be kept in mind by institutions considering the use of AI in lending, servicing, debt collection, marketing, and other regulated activities. The fact that an inaccurate representation or improper action was generated by an AI system rather than a human employee does not eliminate the institution’s responsibility for compliance.
